items.title: Intergr8 Fuels: Global fuel quality remains broadly stable, but localised risks are becoming more important than headline averages
items.original_title: Intergr8 Fuels: Global fuel quality remains broadly stable, but localised risks are becoming more important than headline averages
items.summary: The biannual report, covering fuel quality performance from February to July 2026, finds that global quality averages increasingly mask significant differences between ports, supply chains and fuel characteristics. Changes in crude flows, refinery slates and regional supply pools are contributing to more localised quality exposure. • Localised quality risk: Quality performance varies significantly by port, grade and supply chain, with global averages often masking higher-risk locations and specific quality characteristics. • Biofuel quality: Headline notification rates for biofuel blends remain elevated against conventional ISO reference grades, but much of the apparent exposure is linked to parameters that may not reflect contractual or operational risk. Chris Turner, Technical Manager at Integr8 Fuels: “The headline quality rates tell only part of the story. Risk is increasingly determined by the port, the supply chain and the characteristics of the available fuel pool, rather than by the global average for a grade. Buyers therefore need to look beyond specification and headline price to understand the value and operational implications of the fuel they are actually purchasing.” The report also examines loss control in bunker procurement, showing how energy variance, density differences, additional heating and handling requirements can create costs that remain invisible when fuel is assessed solely against specification limits.

items.title: Port call optimisation pilot projects reveal significant emissions savings potential, new report shows
items.original_title: Port call optimisation pilot projects reveal significant emissions savings potential, new report shows
items.summary: Commercial ships spend between 4% and 6% of their operating year waiting outside ports. That idle time is one of the clearest inefficiencies in shipping, and a combination of slower sailing speeds and port call optimisation can reduce the emissions and fuel currently wasted as ships await an available berth. Instead of sailing fast only to then wait at anchor, port call optimisation allows a ship to arrive when its berth is ready. Cargill Ocean Transportation set out to test the fuel and emissions savings of combining slower sailing speeds with port call optimisation in live commercial operations. With pilot projects at two Australian ports and one in Brazil, the company tested three different mechanisms across 16 voyages and found that the combination can deliver meaningful emissions savings across a range of operational and commercial settings. The findings of the pilots are the subject of a new Global Maritime Forum report, ‘Turning waiting time into savings: Lessons from Cargill’s port call optimisation pilot’. Detailing the pilot projects at the Port of Albany and the Port of Newcastle in Australia, and at Cargill’s grain export terminal in Santarém, Brazil, the report explores the interdependent relationship between port call optimisation and speed reduction.

items.title: IMarEST: From MASS Code to Maritime Practice
items.original_title: IMarEST: From MASS Code to Maritime Practice
items.summary: As shipping becomes increasingly automated, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has introduced legislation to ensure future technology is safe and secure. But there are significant challenges with taking the new Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) Code from policy to practice. The adoption of the International Maritime Organization’s MASS Code marks an important step in the development of maritime autonomy. Adopted at Marine Safety Committee (MSC) 111, it applied as a non-mandatory code from July 2026, with a mandatory code targeted for 2032. This is a sensible approach as maritime autonomy covers everything from small uncrewed survey vessels to large remotely operated ships, and technology is developing too quickly for a regulation built around particular technical solutions. For each relevant requirement, we should be able to trace a path from the intent of the Code through the functions required to satisfy it, the evidence needed to support the claim, and the organisations or individuals responsible for providing and accepting that evidence. Through the MASS SIG, the Institute has an opportunity to convene the maritime autonomy communities around the practical implementation of the Code and capture lessons as autonomous operations move from controlled trials towards routine use. Timing is also important because the current non-mandatory code provides an opportunity to accumulate operational experience before development of the mandatory code progresses.

items.title: Rebounding oil exports through Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to stepped-up Iranian tanker attacks
items.original_title: Rebounding oil exports through Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to stepped-up Iranian tanker attacks
items.summary: Iran has stepped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, threatening a fragile rebound of crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf. Nearly 20 commercial ships, mostly tankers, have come under attack over the past month while sailing through Hormuz, the Persian Gulf or off the coast of Oman, according to the Joint Maritime Information Center, a group of U.S.-allied militaries that provide security updates to merchant vessels. Iran attacked roughly two ships for every 100 vessels that crossed the strait in the third quarter, said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, which tracks ships for defense departments and governments. Shuttle system In many cases, tankers are bringing crude through Hormuz and then transferring the oil onto ships in the Gulf of Oman that haul it to Asia. Crude oil shipments through Hormuz fluctuate daily, sometimes matching or even exceeding levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler, a firm that tracks tankers and global trade flows. Windward estimates crude through Hormuz is averaging 9-10 million bpd compared with a prewar baseline of 14.5 million bpd. High costs But shippers are ferrying crude through Hormuz at high cost to the lives of their crews and in freight and insurance rates, Bockmann said.

items.title: What a 25-Day AIS Blackout Off Libya Tells Us About Mediterranean Narcotics Routes
items.original_title: What a 25-Day AIS Blackout Off Libya Tells Us About Mediterranean Narcotics Routes
items.summary: The 25-Day Gap Between Albania and Libya In late August 2026, a Mali-flagged general cargo vessel left an Albanian port, declared Egypt as its destination, and switched off its AIS transponder in open water off eastern Libya. For 25 days and 8 hours, nothing was transmitted. When it reappeared on September 23, it was at nearly the same position where it had gone dark. What happened off Libya in late August was consistent with a pattern the vessel had been establishing for months. What One Voyage Says About Mediterranean Narcotics Routes What makes this case worth attention is not the single dark activity, but the repeatability built into it. A vessel that returns consistently to the same Albanian base, under a flag with no oversight behind it, with a documented history of going dark off the same coasts, is a vessel whose operational pattern can be run again. The March 2026 Sinai gaps and the August–September Libya gap are consistent with a methodology, not an improvisation. For interdiction and compliance stakeholders tracking Mediterranean narcotics routes, the question is not whether this specific voyage carried something. The vessel that vanished for 25 days off Libya may be one example of a wider operational practice.

Modernising the Registry The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) will launch a new ship registration system in the first half of 2027 to simplify the registration process and make it more seamless for shipowners and ship agents. As at 31 December 2025, the SRS reached a record 137 million gross tonnage (GT), a 27% increase from the previous year, making Singapore the world’s fourth-largest ship registry. With an average vessel age of about 11 years, the SRS is also currently the youngest fleet among the world’s top ten ship registries. items.summary: The World Shipping Council (WSC), in partnership with HUB Ocean, today launched a digital version of the WSC Whale Chart, making global information on measures to protect whales from ships even more accessible. Since its initial launch in 2023, WSC’s Whale Chart was the first global mapping of all known mandatory and voluntary governmental measures designed to reduce harm to whales from vessels. By partnering with HUB Ocean to produce the digital Whale Chart, these measures are now easier to explore, easier to keep up to date, and can plug directly into digital tools and operational systems. Kimberly Mathisen (CEO, HUB Ocean) & Joe Kramek (President & CEO, World Shipping Council) “The Whale Chart has already become an important reference point for the shipping industry,” said Kimberly Mathisen, CEO of HUB Ocean. “Our hope is that by making this information easier to work with, it becomes part of more decisions, more voyages and ultimately more action to protect whales.” The Whale Chart and all its underlying datasets are now available through HUB Ocean’s Ocean Data Platform, an open, cloud-based geospatial platform that turns ocean data into insight and action.

items.original_title: Sanctioned 22-Year-Old Tanker Makes Rare Late-Season Arctic Voyage
items.summary: A 22-year-old product tanker sanctioned by the European Union is making an unusual late-season voyage along Russia’s Northern Sea Route, highlighting the growing use of older, lower-specification vessels to move petroleum products through the Arctic. The Dakar , a 21,300-dwt oil and chemical products tanker built in 2004, is carrying methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a gasoline additive, and appears to be heading west along Russia’s Arctic coast, according vessel tracking data. The cargo was loaded onto another vessel in China in August before being transferred to Dakar off Yeosu, South Korea, in September. That distinguishes it from non-ice-class tankers, while placing it well below the Arc4 and higher ice-class vessels purpose-built for regular Arctic operations. A similar voyage last year demonstrated the risk: the non-ice-class Suezmax Lynx was forced to wait for several day s after encountering sea ice near 72 degrees north while carrying Russian crude toward China. Dakar ’s voyage also follows a sharp increase in Russian oil exports to Asia through the Arctic this year. Reuters reported in August that seven tankers had already moved roughly 6 million barrels of crude through the NSR, nearly half the total shipped by tankers through the route during all of 2025.

The Green Ship Award is presented to vessels and shipowners that have contributed to reducing environmental impact and promoting sustainable maritime transportation in the shipping industry. The two award-winning vessels are equipped with highly environmentally efficient X-DF main engines and embody the “K” LINE Group’s initiatives to reduce environmental impact. Under its long-term environmental guidelines, “K” LINE Environmental Vision 2050 – Blue Seas for the Future -,* “K” LINE Group has set the goal of achieving net-zero GHG emissions by 2050. The “K” LINE Group will continue to promote the development of an environmentally responsible fleet and initiatives to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, while contributing to the resolution of social issues through the provision of sustainable maritime transportation services. items.original_title: Chevron to Divest its Ownership Interests in Hess Midstream and DJ Basin Crude Midstream Assets
items.summary: Chevron Corporation announced that several of its subsidiaries have entered into a series of definitive agreements with Hess Midstream LP (NYSE: HESM) to restructure the terms of its Bakken midstream contracts and establish new DJ Basin midstream contracts. The revised agreements extend the Bakken contracts and are expected to reduce Chevron’s Bakken unit midstream costs by approximately 50%, enhancing future earnings and return on capital employed. In exchange for the improved long-term commercial framework and $200 million in cash consideration, Chevron will transfer to Hess Midstream its ownership interests and general partner position in Hess Midstream, as well as its DJ Basin crude oil midstream assets. As part of this transaction, Chevron expects to fully deconsolidate Hess Midstream, including approximately $3.7 billion of Hess Midstream’s debt. Chevron expects this transaction to be accretive to return on capital employed by 0.5% on an absolute basis and generate long-term future economic value through a lower cost structure and improved earnings. At closing, Chevron expects to recognize a one-time after-tax loss estimated at approximately $3 to $4 billion,1 given that the company is unable to recognize future Bakken midstream cost savings as an asset. “This transaction resets the commercial framework between our upstream and midstream assets in the Bakken and DJ Basins,” said Andy Walz, Chevron’s President of Downstream, Midstream and Chemicals.

items.original_title: Trafigura Buys Seven Oil Tankers From SFL as Shipping Costs Rise
items.summary: Trafigura Group bought seven oil tankers from New York-listed SFL Corp., in the latest example of how trading houses and state energy companies are acquiring vessels to ship crude and products. Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have drawn in scores of tankers to shuttle key oil flows out to the global market, while growing risks in the Red Sea are leading to longer voyage routes and times. That’s prompted a rush to snap up tankers as rates to charter vessels soar. Trafigura bought four oil product tankers known as LR2s — built in 2014 and 2015 — and three suezmax tankers built in 2019, SFL said in a statement on Wednesday. SFL said it had made an “aggregate book gain” of $175 million from the deal, without disclosing the sale price of the vessels. Strong demand for prompt availability of oil carriers have pushed the resale values of tankers higher. A 10-year-old Aframax, which is the same size as an LR2 tanker, was assessed to be worth $72.5 million last week, while a Suezmax of the same age could sell for $110 million, Clarkson data show. Trafigura recently made its first foray into launching a public company, listing a supertanker vehicle Volare Shipping Ltd.

Workers have won: a 3.4% wage increase for the next year, backdated to 1 August; a €200 increase in holiday pay; and dockers involved in “high-turnover container operations” will receive an additional annual lump sum, increased by €416 from 1 January. “It was a difficult round, but the bottom line was acceptable,” added ver.di, while union officials said a 24-hour ‘warning strike’ by members in mid-August had been the catalyst for this week’s agreement. The agreement staves off the potential for further cargo backlogs building in Germany’s three main container gateways of Hamburg, Bremerhaven, and Wilhelmshaven – although shippers and freight forwarders are still encountering some congestion. However, German shippers in the central Rhine industrial belt continue to face hinterland congestion caused by low water levels on the Rhine, and the subsequent restrictions on barge movements to the key gateways of Rotterdam and Antwerp.

The stoppage has already left some 150 tonnes of Indian exports for Russia – primarily pharmaceuticals, machinery, and spare parts – stranded over the past week. And India-Russia trade disruption is not limited to air freight: container carriers have also stopped accepting bookings from India to Russia’s Novorossiysk port, a major hub in the Black Sea, over fears of escalating drone attacks on vessels, as well as other growing security risks in the region, sources told The Loadstar . items.summary: Eight planned sailings carried high-value exports through the Northern Sea Route, with service to resume next summer. China has completed the first season of regular weekly container shipping between China and Europe via the Northern Sea Route, with the operator completing all eight sailings planned for 2026 before ending departures slightly earlier than scheduled because of Arctic ice forecasts. Sea Legend Shipping launched its China-Europe Arctic Express in Augus t, deploying seven ice-strengthened container ships for eight weekly westbound voyages from Ningbo-Zhoushan and other Chinese ports. The season carried more than 14,000 twenty-foot equivalent units of export cargo across the eight voyages, according to preliminary figures reported by Zhejiang authorities. The first voyage of the season by Dubai Tower carried 1,370 TEUs from Ningbo, Shanghai, Taicang and Qingdao to Europe. The Arctic route takes about 18 to 20 days between China and Northern Europe, roughly half the transit time of traditional routes via the Suez Canal, according to Chinese transport authorities. The end of Sea Legend’s departures does not mark the end of Chinese container activity on the Northern Sea Route for 2026. The completion of all eight planned voyages marks a step beyond last year’s experimental voyages, when the Sea Legend service was still testing the commercial and operational feasibility of Arctic container shipping.

items.summary: Seven major ports across Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany have secured government backing for a wider cross-border programme aimed at cutting regulatory barriers and accelerating automated freight and energy infrastructure across the Antwerp-Rotterdam-Rhine-Ruhr corridor. One of the more concrete logistics measures is a plan to use cross-border corridors such as Antwerp-Rotterdam for automated freight transport by road and inland waterway. Ports in the region have also been pushing for so-called acceleration areas to shorten planning and permitting times for major infrastructure and industrial projects. That call has now been incorporated into the summit declaration, alongside moves to reduce regulatory differences between the three jurisdictions. The three governments will take the programme to Brussels, asking the European Commission to recognise the Antwerp-Rotterdam-Rhine-Ruhr Area, or ARRRA, as a strategic European port-industrial cluster.

The decline has been largely offset by Singapore’s bunker premium over JKM, which has gone from $4.31/MMBtu ($224/mt) a week ago to $4.41/MMBtu ($229/mt). items.title: ShipGod AI: Why every vessel needs its own digital memory
items.original_title: ShipGod AI: Why every vessel needs its own digital memory
items.summary: After four decades at sea and ashore, Bing Hou has reached a simple conclusion about shipmanagement: too much of what keeps vessels safe still depends on paper, spreadsheets and what individual seafarers happen to remember. The 56-year-old master mariner, founder of ShipGod AI, spends 25 years with China Yangtze Shipping, rising from deck cadet to Class-1 ocean-going master and serving on everything from containerships and tankers to LNG carriers, passenger ships and offshore vessels. Since 2016, Hou has worked ashore in marine management, ship surveying, DPA roles and teaching. “ISM got the principle right decades ago: every ship must operate its own Safety Management System, fitted to that specific ship. That frustration became the basis for ShipGod AI, which he describes as an offline-first workspace giving each vessel its own digital environment and AI assistant. Every ship, its own system. ShipGod AI instead allows companies to mirror their existing safety management structures while giving each vessel its own documents, checklists, records, inspections and equipment history. The AI runs locally onboard and answers from the ship’s own information rather than the wider internet. As a young seafarer in the 1980s, Hou listened to shortwave radio during long voyages and dreamt of creating a station for seafarers.

items.title: Bunker prices jump by three-quarters since Iran war began
items.original_title: Bunker prices jump by three-quarters since Iran war began
items.summary: The cost of fuelling ships has risen by roughly three-quarters since the US-Iran war erupted on February 28. In Singapore, the world’s largest bunkering hub, VLSFO was assessed by ENGINE at $509 per tonne on February 27, the final trading day before the war began, while high-sulphur fuel oil stood at $432 per tonne. By Monday this week, VLSFO had climbed to $886 per tonne and HSFO to $764, increases of 74% and 77% respectively. Prices initially went vertical after US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and the subsequent disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Ship & Bunker data shows Singapore VLSFO rising from $521.50 per tonne immediately before the conflict to a peak of $1,120.50 by March 13. The market subsequently retreated as supply chains adjusted and hopes periodically surfaced of a diplomatic breakthrough, but bunker prices have never returned close to their pre-war levels, and have been increasing again in recent weeks. In Singapore, the absolute discount enjoyed by scrubber-fitted ships burning HSFO has widened from around $77 per tonne immediately before the war to roughly $122 today, even though the price of HSFO itself has surged.

items.original_title: Iran’s Offshore Oil Stockpile Nears Exhaustion as Blockade Chokes New Supply
items.summary: Iran’s offshore crude stockpile in Southeast Asia is being rapidly depleted as the U.S. maritime blockade prevents fresh barrels from leaving the Persian Gulf, according to new tracking data from United Against Nuclear Iran. UANI said an estimated 9 million barrels of Iranian crude were transferred through ship-to-ship operations in waters off Malaysia during September, drawing down inventories accumulated before the blockade took effect. “Given that no Iranian crude has made it past the blockade line, Iran’s offshore floating storage in the South China Sea is rapidly dwindling,” the group said. The crude transfers totaled an estimated 9 million barrels and were ultimately destined for Chinese independent refiners, commonly known as “teapots.” The activity has continued despite growing scrutiny of the large network of sanctioned and Iran-linked vessels operating in the region. The depletion of offshore storage comes even as oil exports from other Persian Gulf producers have recovered. If UANI’s estimate of roughly 10 million barrels remaining in Malaysian floating storage is accurate, the pool of crude available outside the blockade has fallen sharply. With no new crude reaching those offshore inventories, continued deliveries to China would increasingly depend on drawing down a finite stockpile rather than replacing exported barrels.

items.summary: File Photo: Oil tanker Al Shaffiah sails at the sea near the Omani coast, as seen from Musandam, Oman, June 26, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer LONDON, Oct 6 – Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged to over 81% of pre- war levels in September, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports despite attacks on the kingdom’s oil infrastructure and escalating Iranian attacks on regional shipping, while Iranian exports fell to zero due to a US blockade. The blockade has all but choked off Iranian exports, while other Gulf producers have adapted to attacks on energy infrastructure and shipping by relying on so-called dark transits — switching off tankers’ tracking systems to evade detection — to protect the oil flows that underpin their economies. Flows of crude, condensate and refined fuels including LPG averaged 19.2 million barrels per day (bpd) from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Iraq and the UAE, Vortexa data showed, compared with an average of about 23.6 million bpd in the year that preceded the outbreak of the Iran war on February 28. Crude and condensate flows recovered to 91% of their pre-war levels of 16.3 million bpd, Vortexa data showed.

The pipeline, which transports crude to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu, has not experienced any interruptions, a source said Monday. The statement came after media reports suggested a recent disruption amid ongoing tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis. Saudi Arabia restarted the pipeline operations following drone attacks on September 11 that forced the kingdom to shut down the pipeline and halt crude loadings at Yanbu, three sources briefed on the matter said. items.title: Europe’s diesel tightness persists into Q4
items.original_title: Europe’s diesel tightness persists into Q4
items.summary: Europe’s diesel/gasoil imports from outside the region hit the lowest September on record. Diesel/gasoil exports pointed to Europe from outside regions averaged only 1mbd in September, down 600kbd y-o-y. Russia and the Middle East account for most of the drop, together down 580kbd compared to last year. Diesel on the water pointed to Europe is more than 25% below last year’s levels, all points indicating that October will be another month of weak arrivals. Europe’s implied refinery runs fell by around 600kbd in September (according to our estimates), after reaching a year-to-date high in August. Strong margins have delayed maintenance at key refineries into 2027, including Tarragona (180kbd), Thessaloniki (66kbd) and Gonfreville (247kbd) (Argus), so maintenance season is likely to already have peaked in September this year, as opposed to the usual October. The US is still the key external supplier The US supplied 41% of Europe’s external diesel in September, at 400kbd, above year-ago levels but down from a dataset high of 445kbd in August. A growing portion of China’s diesel cargoes are moving on LR2s. Unless Asia’s diesel arb to Europe widens, China’s Q4 barrels will likely keep prioritising shorter-haul destinations amid high freight costs.

Still, the near-term demand outlook remains constrained by signs of weakening industrial activity in China, the world’s largest consumer of the metal. On the supply side, Chilean copper output dropped in August to its lowest level since February 2011, while workers at Antofagasta’s Centinela mine voted in favor of strike action after wage negotiations failed to reach an agreement. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has yet to decide on potential tariffs targeting refined copper. Earlier threats of US duties on refined metals encouraged traders to divert shipments toward American warehouses, contributing to the recent surge in copper prices. Source: Trading Economics

Middle East LNG export volumes and weather patterns continue to drive the market outlook. The firm’s analysis focuses on the combination of supply constraints from the Persian Gulf region and potential demand increases from colder-than-normal winter conditions. The upside risk assessment reflects the possibility of both factors materializing together.

items.title: d’Amico brings last leased tanker back in-house
items.original_title: d’Amico brings last leased tanker back in-house
items.summary: Italian product tanker owner d’Amico International Shipping has exercised a $14m purchase option on the 2014-built MR tanker High Fidelity , paving the way for its entire operating fleet to return to full ownership. Operating arm d’Amico Tankers is expected to take ownership of the 50,000 dwt Hyundai Vinashin-built vessel around mid-January 2027, with the final price subject to a small adjustment depending on the actual transfer date. The ship is one of the last two vessels in d’Amico’s fleet still operating under bareboat arrangements. The company currently controls 28 product tankers on the water — 16 MRs, six handysizes and six LR1s — comprising 26 owned ships and two bareboat-chartered units. The move follows d’Amico’s decision in August to exercise a $15.3m option on sister-era MR High Discovery, which is due to return to full ownership in November. Once both transfers are completed, d’Amico will have no remaining bareboat-chartered ships. Both vessels were refinanced through sale-and-leaseback structures in 2022. At the time, d’Amico exercised previous options on High Discovery and High Fidelity for $20.3m and $19.2m respectively before refinancing them under new 10-year bareboat leases containing fresh purchase options. D’Amico meanwhile has 10 newbuildings on order, comprising four LR1s due in 2027 and six smaller product tankers — two handysizes and four MRs — lined up for 2029.

items.title: HD Hyundai delivers world’s first lashing-free containership
items.original_title: HD Hyundai delivers world’s first lashing-free containership
items.summary: HD Hyundai has delivered what it says is the world’s first containership designed to eliminate manual lashing, removing one of the most labour-intensive jobs in container shipping. The 13,000 teu vessel, which is methanol dual-fuelled, has been handed over toFrance’s CMA CGM after being built using HD Hyundai’s proprietary hybrid lashing-free system. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries developed and verified the core technology, while HD Hyundai Samho carried out detailed design and construction. HD Hyundai’s new arrangement does away with that work by extending cell guides above deck, allowing containers to be held in place without traditional lashing. The breakthrough centres on what HD Hyundai calls a portable bench, a standardised structure fitted between cell guides. The unit is the same size as a 40 ft container, meaning terminal cranes can handle it as part of normal cargo operations. HD Hyundai says the design boosts deck cargo capacity by more than 10% compared with similar existing ships while improving operational stability in heavy weather. The technology was presented to the IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers in 2024 and has since secured multiple patents. The Korean yard plans to expand the lashing-free technology to small and mid-sized vessels soon.

Two seafarers were killed and 11 rescued. If the Bulgarian reports are confirmed, the latest incidents would mark a significant westward expansion of the threat facing merchant shipping in the Black Sea, taking the danger well beyond waters immediately off Ukraine. The attacks also come just as Turkey and the United Nations are trying to revive talks aimed at securing a limited Black Sea maritime truce. Ankara has been pushing a framework focused on protecting commercial navigation, ports and energy infrastructure, drawing in part on the architecture of the former Black Sea Grain Initiative.

items.title: Panama Canal extends long-term slot system to panamax locks
items.original_title: Panama Canal extends long-term slot system to panamax locks
items.summary: The Panama Canal is extending its long-term slot allocation programme to the Panamax locks for the first time as it looks to give more customers greater certainty through the coming dry season. The new Long-term Slot Allocation, or LoTSA, phase will cover January 3 to April 3, 2027, with the established neopanamax system running alongside a new panamax pilot. For neopanamax vessels, 36 packages covering 270 slots will be offered, split between 165 northbound and 105 southbound passages. The panamax pilot will offer 51 packages and 288 slots, evenly spread at roughly three transits per day. The move builds on a system first introduced for the larger locks in 2024, when the Panama Canal Authority began offering blocks of future reservations to customers seeking greater scheduling certainty after the severe 2023-24 drought. Splash reported in May that neopanamax auction prices had surged to as much as $4m as Middle East disruption redirected more US energy cargoes through Panama. By August, one LPG carrier had paid a record $5.3m for priority passage as deteriorating water conditions and strong demand squeezed capacity. The canal subsequently cut daily booking capacity to 32 ships and tightened draft limits as rainfall disappointed, before recent rains allowed some restrictions to be eased again.

items.title: How close is shipping to the top?
items.original_title: How close is shipping to the top?
items.summary: Shipping markets rarely announce the top with any clarity. More often, the argument about whether the peak has arrived only really starts when freight rates are still climbing, asset values are making less and less conventional sense and owners are sufficiently confident to keep buying ships at prices that would have looked ridiculous a few months earlier. Chief correspondent Adis Adjin assesses where we are in today’s record high shipping cycle. But there are enough signs beneath the surface to start asking a more awkward question: how much of this cycle is left, and which sectors are closest to finding out? The comparison with the last supercycle has its limits — today’s orderbook is equivalent to around 23% of the fleet, against more than 50% at the 2008 peak — but the direction of travel is clear. The bigger issue is what happens to the amount of large tonnage still scheduled to emerge from Asian yards, much of it above 12,000 teu, while a large share of the chartered fleet that can be returned sits below 8,000 teu. Around 14% of current capacity is due to arrive before the end of the decade, while recycling potential amounts to roughly 8% of today’s fleet.

items.summary: Hambantota International Port (HIP) has surpassed one million TEUs in cumulative container throughput since the commissioning of new quay cranes in 2025, marking a significant milestone in the rapid growth of its container operations. The achievement reflects the continued expansion of HIP’s container business and growing customer confidence in its operational capabilities. “Crossing one million TEUs is an important achievement for HIP and a strong indication of the confidence our customers are placing in the port. In April, HIP established a new single-vessel handling record when the MSC Marie Leslie recorded 7,968 container moves, equivalent to 13,260 TEUs, during its call at the port. HIP subsequently achieved its highest-ever monthly container throughput in June, handling 80,325 TEUs. Central to the programme are six new quay cranes and 16 rubber-tyred gantry cranes, forming part of the port’s wider USD 108 million investment in container-handling machinery and supporting assets. “The one-million-TEU milestone shows that HIP’s container business is moving into a new stage of growth. items.title: Strong Freight Markets Keep Aging Ships Out of Recycling Yards
items.original_title: Strong Freight Markets Keep Aging Ships Out of Recycling Yards
items.summary: Strong freight markets kept aging vessels trading through the third quarter despite rising scrap prices and strong demand from ship recyclers, according to a new market review from GMS, the world’s largest cash buyer of ships for recycling. The ship recycling market entered the quarter looking ripe for an increase in demolition activity. GMS said it was tracking roughly 550 merchant vessels preparing to exit the Gulf at the start of July, including around 200 bulk carriers, while recycling yards in the major South Asian markets had available capacity and appetite for tonnage. The report argues that owners were weighing recycling offers against a much broader set of alternatives, including freight earnings, secondhand sale opportunities, remaining vessel life, route risks and compliance costs. GMS expects recycling supply to remain tight into the fourth quarter as long as vessel earnings remain strong, particularly where ships continue to find lucrative employment linked to the Strait of Hormuz. But those delayed recycling decisions may be creating a larger pool of aging tonnage that will eventually need to leave the fleet. If freight earnings normalize, secondhand liquidity weakens or employment opportunities narrow, GMS said some of that deferred supply could reach recycling markets over a much shorter period.

As RED III applies to all industries, there will also be competition from the airline and heavy transport industries in the use of bio-residues, and we suspect this will create additional risksin the maritime sector. Buyers in the sector may be exposed to lower-quality residues, for example, chemically variable feedstocks and/or blends from multiple residue streams. Pressure may mount on traceability systems, fraud risks may increase (due to misclassification of sustainabilityvalues in Proof of Compliance documents) and disputes over the chain of custodyaccumulate. items.original_title: LNG Trade Through Hormuz Extends Rebound Despite Shipping Risks
items.summary: LNG carriers at the Qatari LNG export facility at Ras Laffan. Photo: RasGas Oct 5, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Shipments of liquefied natural gas through the Strait of Hormuz extended a rebound that began in September, as the region’s producers seek to restore supplies to energy-starved customers. At least three LNG shipments have exited the key waterway since late last week, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg and Kpler. The market is closely watching LNG shipments through Hormuz for signs of relief from a supply crunch that last month pushed prices in Europe and Asia to the highest since late 2022. The increase in traffic comes as risks to shipping remain acute following a flurry of incidents in recent days. UK Maritime Trade Operations said it received a report of a tanker being hit by an unknown projectile within Hormuz on Oct 4. US President Donald Trump's push to steer $54 billion of South Korean investment into Alaska LNG is putting a fresh focus on a 20 million-ton-a-year export project that would cost more than twice as much as a comparable US Gulf Coast plant. items.original_title: U-Ming doubles down in China with six-ship bulker spend
items.summary: Taiwan’s U-Ming Marine Transport has committed up to $312m on six more bulkers in China, adding four ultramaxes and firming another pair of Newcastlemaxes as it presses ahead with plans to build a 100-ship fleet. Two separate Taiwan exchange disclosures from U-Ming’s Singapore subsidiary put the combined investment at between $296m and $312m. The larger ships are two 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes at Jiangsu Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, priced at between $77m and $80m each for a total of $154m to $160m. U-Ming is also paying between $142m and $152m for four 64,000 dwt ultramaxes at Sumec Marine-controlled New Dayang Shipbuilding, equating to $35.5m to $38m per ship. The first of the ultramaxes is scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2029, with the remaining three following during 2030. The latest contracting advances an expansion plan approved by U-Ming earlier this year covering four 210,000 dwt bulkers and four ultramaxes. U-Ming has been steadily renewing and expanding its core dry bulk fleet while moving into new sectors. At its May investor presentation, the company was targeting a fleet of more than 100 vessels, with dry bulk remaining at the centre of the expansion. U-Ming said at the end of September that its owned, joint venture and newbuilding fleet had reached around 90 ships and passed the 10m dwt mark.

items.title: South Korea-Russia ocean volumes boosted by rail congestion in China
items.original_title: South Korea-Russia ocean volumes boosted by rail congestion in China
items.summary: Growing congestion along the Trans-China and Trans-Siberian railways, linking China and Russia, has boosted South Korea-Russia container volumes, encouraging shipping lines to consider deploying larger vessels this month. In August, more than 33,000 teu was transported from Busan to ports in Russia’s far east, such as Vladivostok, a slight increase on July. Of this, exports, excluding transhipment cargo, were 8,000 teu. Volumes are said to have remained at the same level in September, as South Korean shippers rushed to get cargo out before the country’s Thanksgiving Day holiday on 25-26 September and China’s week-long National Day on 1 October. Consequently, cargo “rollovers”, where shipments are delayed due to a lack of space, are becoming increasingly frequent and Busan-Vladivostok freight rates now average $1,700 per teu, up from $1,500 per teu in August, which had seen a $300 jump from July. A representative at Dong Young Shipping, which offers South Korea-Russia services, said: “We’re considering deploying larger vessels than those currently in use, so we can offer more slots.” Congestion around major Chinese hub ports following the East Asia typhoon season in August resulted in more Chinese shippers opting for rail freight to Europe. And as rail capacity has failed to keep pace with the surge in cargo volume, waiting times for train departures now exceed one week.

items.title: Empty box pile-up at port of Manila sparks truckers’ strike
items.original_title: Empty box pile-up at port of Manila sparks truckers’ strike
items.summary: Customs brokers and hauliers are expected to voluntarily stop work today in advance of a three-day trucking strike in Manila, as a year-long standoff on carriers failing to remove their empties reaches its limit – Hapag-Lloyd having suspended bookings amid the chaos. Warning the protest could “last a week”, Reynaldo Soliman, chair of the Practicing Customs Brokers and Port Truckers Alliance, urged brokers not to secure gate passes, book trucks, or release shipments, until carriers reduced the number of empties at Manila. “Even though we want to ship, we cannot move,” Mr Soliman told local reporters, with the number of empties scattered around terminals, hauliers yards, and waiting on flatbeds to be removed, measured in the thousands with just 10% of volumes moving out of Manila’s ports. In a letter seen by The Loadstar , Bureau of Customs commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno told Port of Manila it needed to take measures to address the worsening empties backlog, suggesting boxes that had been waiting for more than 10 days be moved offsite. “Increasing yard utilisation levels at the Manila International Container Port and the port of Manila continue to adversely affect the efficient movement of cargo and the overall flow of port operations,” he wrote.

items.title: South Africa’s port reform takes an important step forward
items.original_title: South Africa’s port reform takes an important step forward
items.summary: One battle doesn’t win a war, but just getting to a stage where South Africa’s port system can now be reformed is an achievement by itself. The decision of South Africa’s government to formally endorse the separation of Transnet National Port Authority (TNPA), the country’s de facto port landlord, from the Transnet rail operations is a step in the right direction – one that its shippers, forwarders, and other supply chain stakeholders have been demanding for years. Operations at South Africa’s key container gateways of Durban, Cape Town, Coega and Port Elizabeth have been plagued by congestion and delays for years. And while it’s great the government has finally kicked off the reform process of Transnet, it also means some of the really hard work begins now, as the South African Association of Freight Forwarders argues when it says the real imperative is “getting corporatisation right”. The central point of the reform is that TNPA will be moved out of the Transnet group – which will continue to manage Transnet Port Terminals, but with much reduced investment power – and become a standalone state organisation with the ability to take its own investment decisions on both infrastructure and superstructure, and independently manage landlord revenues.
